summary.text: India produces approximately 20.5 to 21.0 million metric tonnes (MT) of mangoes annually, with national output totaling roughly 62.5 million MT across the recent three crop cycles (2021–22 to 2023–24). Production is heavily concentrated in two major belts: the subtropical Gangetic plain (led by Uttar Pradesh and Bihar) and the tropical southern peninsula (led by Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Telangana).

passages.text: Chittoor & Tirupati Belt (~32–36% of state output): The primary hub for Totapuri, feeding India’s largest aseptic fruit pulp processing and export corridor.
Krishna & NTR Districts (~22–26%): Concentrated around Nuzvid and Vijayawada; primary production zone for table-grade Banganapalli (Benishan).
Kadapa (YSR) & Annamayya (~12–15%): Major mid-to-late harvest tract.
Remaining Districts (~23–34%): Kurnool, West Godavari, and Visakhapatnam.
Lucknow Belt (~22–25% of state output): Anchored by the Malihabad–Kakori belt; accounts for the core volume of Dasheri and Lucknow Safeda.
Saharanpur & Muzaffarnagar (~20–24%): Northern commercial belt specializing in late-season table varieties, mainly Chausa and Langra.
Varanasi & Mirzapur (~10–13%): Eastern agro-climatic pocket famous for Banarasi Langra.
Bulandshahr, Unnao & Sitapur (~15–18%): Expanding orchards supplying Delhi-NCR and northern mandis.
Remaining Districts (~20–33%): Bareilly, Barabanki, and Hardoi.
Kolar & Chikkaballapura (~42–48% of state output): Srinivaspur is the largest processing cluster in South India, supplying large quantities of Totapuri and Badami.
Ramanagara & Bengaluru Rural (~18–22%): Major center for Raspuri and fresh-market Alphonso.
Dharwad & Belagavi (~10–14%): Northern transitional belt contributing substantial table-grade fruit.
Remaining Districts (~16–30%): Tumakuru, Mandya, and Hassan.
Darbhanga, Madhubani & Samastipur (~30–35% of state output): Mithila belt, heavy concentration of traditional Malda and local cultivars.
Bhagalpur (~18–22%): GI tract for Zardalu and prominent pocket for commercial Langra
Muzaffarpur & Vaishali (~16–20%): Gangetic alluvial belt with mixed orchards.
Remaining Districts (~23–36%): West Champaran, Rohtas, and Patna.
Junagadh & Gir Somnath (~45–52% of state output): Foothills of Girnar, the designated GI zone for premium Gir Kesar.
Valsad & Navsari (~26–30%): South Gujarat coastal belt, primarily cultivating Valsad Alphonso and Rajapuri.
Kutch (~10–14%): Arid-zone late harvest Kesar cluster.
Remaining Districts (~4–19%): Amreli, Bhavnagar, and Surat.
Malda (~55–60% of state output): The state’s primary mango cluster (English Bazar, Ratua, Kaliachak), leading in Fazli, Himsagar, and Laxmanbhog.
Murshidabad (~20–25%): Historical orchard belt centered around Jiaganj and Lalbagh.
Nadia & North 24 Parganas (~10–14%): Major commercial sources for early-market Himsagar and Bombai.
Remaining Districts (~1–15%): Hooghly and Bankura.

7. Telangana-Across the recent three seasons, Telangana produced approximately 2.7 to 2.9 million metric tonnes (MT) of mangoes combined, averaging between 900,000 and 1,000,000 MT per year. The state accounts for roughly 4.5% of India's total mango production.

The varietal mix is overwhelmingly dominated by Banganapalli (Benishan), which covers around 75–80% of total acreage, followed by Dasheri (~10%), Himayat / Imam Pasand (~2–3%), and local juicy varieties (such as Cherukurasam and Peddarasam).

Eastern Basin,Khammam & Bhadradri Kothagudem,~24% – 28%,Leading commercial volume hub; heavy production of high-grade Banganapalli and juicy varieties; feeds both Hyderabad processing units and export consolidators.
Northern Plateau,Jagtial & Mancherial,~18% – 22%,Anchored by the Jagtial mango hub; prime region for early-to-mid season Benishan and high-sugar-content table fruit.
Southern Drylands,Nagarkurnool & Mahabubnagar,~14% – 17%,Red chalka soils favorable for orchard longevity; prominent source for early-harvest Banganapalli and Dasheri.

Peri-Urban Corridor,Sangareddy & Rangareddy,~12% – 15%,Traditional cultivation pockets around Zaheerabad and Chevella; known for high-value table varieties including Himayat and direct farm-to-mandi supply for Greater Hyderabad.
Central Plains,Siddipet & Mahabubabad,~10% – 12%,Substantial mid-season arrivals; expanding high-density plantation areas.
Other Districts,"Nalgonda, Suryapet, Karimnagar, Jangaon, etc.",~10% – 15%,Dispersed orchards primarily supplying local APMC mandis.

context: State-Wise & Variety-Wise Market Availability Calendar
The Indian harvest cycle shifts geographically from south to north, starting in peninsular India by late February/March and concluding in the northern Gangetic plains by August.
Key Table Varieties, Belts & Primary Export Destinations

Export protocols are governed by phytosanitary treatments: Vapor Heat Treatment (VHT) for Japan/South Korea, and Irradiation (Gamma ray at 400 Gy minimum) for the USA and Australia to control fruit flies (Bactrocera dorsalis) and stone weevils (Sternochetus mangiferae).
Key Processed Products & Production Breakdown Estimates
India processes approximately 1.8 to 2.2 million MT of fresh mangoes annually into value-added derivatives, anchored by Aseptic Mango Pulp/Puree packed in 215 kg bag-in-drum formats.
Key Processed Formats:
Totapuri Mango Concentrate (TMC): Concentrated under vacuum to 28° Brix; global standard base for commercial nectars, multi-fruit blends, and re-dilution beverages.
Totapuri Mango Pulp (TMP): Single-strength, natural pulp pasteurized at 14° Brix; high fiber-matrix stability and high yield.
Alphonso Mango Pulp (AMP): Natural single-strength (16–18° Brix) and sweetened pulp; luxury aromatic base for ice cream, high-end pure juices, and confectionery.
Kesar Mango Pulp (KMP): High color density (deep orange-yellow) and balanced acidity (16–17° Brix); popular for dairy blending, RTDs, and Indian diaspora baking segments.
IQF Dices/Slices & Canned Slices: Frozen chunks and canned slices in light/heavy syrup for foodservice and bakery applications.
Estimated Share of Processed Mango Production & Pulp Output in India
Total Aseptic Pulp & Concentrate Production: ~550,000 – 650,000 MT/year
[▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓]                             ~18% - 22%  Alphonso Mango Pulp (AMP)
[▓▓▓▓]                                     ~6% - 8%   Kesar Mango Pulp (KMP)

Totapuri dominates total processing volume due to its exceptionally high processing recovery (42–48% pulp yield), disease tolerance, and low cost-per-ton.
Alphonso and Kesar dominate total export value, trading at a price premium of 150% to 250% over Totapuri per metric ton.

Chittoor Processing Cluster (Andhra Pradesh)
Primary Products: Totapuri Mango Concentrate (TMC), Totapuri Mango Pulp (TMP), Banganapalli Puree.
Catchment Area: Bangarupalyam, Damalcheruvu, Palamaner, Kuppam, Madanapalle; cross-border arrivals from Vellore (TN) and Kolar (KA).
Infrastructure: 60+ processing facilities (e.g., Capricorn, Galla Foods/Amara Raja, Jain Farm Fresh).
Krishnagiri–Dharmapuri Cluster (Tamil Nadu)
Primary Products: TMP, TMC, Alphonso Mango Pulp (southern crop), Organic Mango Puree.
Catchment Area: Krishnagiri, Barugur, Pochampalli, Kaveripattinam, Rayakottai, Dharmapuri, Salem belt; Srinivaspur mandi (Karnataka).
Infrastructure: Over 75 aseptic packing and canning units; acts as the primary export feeder via Chennai and Tuticorin ports.
Konkan Coast Cluster (Maharashtra)
Primary Products: Natural Alphonso Pulp (AMP), Sweetened Canned Pulp, Single-strength puree.
Catchment Area: Ratnagiri, Sindhudurg (Devgad, Vengurla), Raigad (Alibag, Murud), extended to Sangli/Kolhapur for intermediate handling.
Infrastructure: Export-centric units oriented toward JNPT (Nhava Sheva) shipping lanes; certified BRC/FSSC facilities catering to European/US diasporas.
Saurashtra & South Gujarat Cluster (Gujarat)
Primary Products: Kesar Mango Pulp (KMP), Rajapuri Chunks, Alphonso blends.
Catchment Area: Talala Gir, Junagadh, Dhari, Kodinar, Una, Navsari, Valsad, and Gandevi.
Infrastructure: Hubs in Talala, Junagadh, Valsad, and Vadodara feeding exports via Kandla and Mundra ports.
Crop Phenology & Climatic Parameters
The phenological progression of mango spans 120 to 160 days from bloom to harvest, depending on variety and ambient heat units.
Dormancy / Rest       Flower Induction       Full Bloom & Fruit Set     Pea to Marble Stage       Stone Hardening         Maturity & Ripening
[Oct – Nov / Dec]  ──►  [Dec – Jan]    ──►   [Jan – Feb / Mar]   ──►    [Feb – Mar / Apr]   ──►  [Mar – Apr / May]  ──►   [Apr – Jun / Jul]
~60–75 Days            ~30–45 Days            ~20–25 Days                ~30–40 Days              ~25–35 Days               ~25–35 Days
Detailed Phenological Breakdown
Vegetative Rest / Flower Bud Induction (October – December; 60–75 days)
Phenology: Terminal shoots stop flushing; carbohydrates accumulate in mature leaves.
Ideal Climate: Low night temperatures (10–15°C) and a strict dry spell (soil moisture deficit) of at least 6–8 weeks to trigger floral induction over vegetative growth.
Risk: Unseasonal winter rains or excessive nitrogen fertility induce unwanted vegetative flushes instead of flower panicles.
Panicle Emergence to Full Bloom (December – February; 30–45 days)
Phenology: Panicle elongation, opening of staminate and hermaphrodite flowers; pollination occurs (predominantly entomophilous via Diptera species like Musca domestica).
Ideal Climate: 22–28°C daytime temperature, dry weather, relative humidity 50–65%.
Risk: Temperatures below 10°C cause embryo abortion, resulting in stenospermocarpic ("pocket") fruit; rain or morning mist causes blossom blight and powdery mildew.
Fruit Set & Pea-to-Marble Development (January – March; 30–40 days)
Phenology: Post-pollination ovary swell, massive natural drop (98–99% abscission of initial set); remaining fruitlets advance from pin-head to pea and marble sizes.
Ideal Climate: 25–32°C, moderate humidity.
Management: Critical stage for supplemental drip irrigation to prevent heavy fruit abscission.
Stone Hardening Stage (March – April; 25–35 days)
Phenology: Rapid cell enlargement slows; endocarp lignifies and hardens into stone; mesocarp accumulates starch reserves.
Ideal Climate: 30–36°C, dry sunny days.
Vulnerability: Sensitive to sudden swings in soil moisture, which cause physiological fruit splitting.
Physiological Maturity & Ripening (April – July; 25–35 days)
Phenology: Shoulder rise above stem attachment, depression of stalk cavity, peel color change from dark olive green to pale/yellowish, specific gravity reaching 1.01–1.02.
Ideal Climate: 32–38°C; high sunshine hours accelerate TSS (°Brix) accumulation and carotenoid synthesis.
Risk: Pre-harvest rains at this stage introduce fruit fly infestation and post-harvest anthracnose/stem-end rot.
Phytosanitary Matrix: Major Pests, Diseases & Management
